newsitem.title: USA: Bidding for GM Hughes continues, deal seen soon - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bidding for GM Hughes continues, deal seen soon - analysts.

text.p: The multibillion-dollar tug of war for Hughes Electronics Corp. between Northrop Grumman Corp. and Raytheon Co. intensified as bids rose for the General Motors Corp. unit's missile and radar business, sources said Friday.
Sources following the auction said the bids now stand in the range of $9.8 billion to $10.4 billion.
Lexington, Mass.-based Raytheon initially bid $9 billion, while Northrop Grumman, based in Los Angeles, offered $9.2 billion, sources said.
The Boston Globe reported that both companies raised their bids to $10 billion and GM's board was meeting Friday to study them.
All the companies involved declined to comment.
"I think the final bids are in," said Roger Threlfall, an analyst at J.P. Morgan. "GM will (likely) make a decision before the markets open on Monday or early Monday morning."
Paul Nisbet of JSA Research said a deal "is very imminent."
The winner of the bidding war will emerge as the premier firm in the defence electronics business.

GM's H class stock, which reflects the performance of Hughes Electronics, closed unchanged at $63.125 on the New York Stock Exchange. Northrop stock dropped 12.5 cents to $77.75 and Raytheon fell 25 cents to $47.75, also on the NYSE.

"I don't think price is the real determinant," Nisbet said. "If the price is too high, it's going to be detrimental to the stock performance of the winning bidder. ... GM will want a stock that performs well."

Analysts expect GM will take as much as $6 billion worth of stock from the winning bidder. To avoid a hefty tax bill, it has to hold those shares for a few years, so the future share price of the winner is crucial to the deal.
"Plans to repair their balance sheet after a buyout of Hughes will be of more interest than whether (GM) gets another $100 million or $200 million in price," Nisbet said.
The winning side will probably divest and carry out layoffs, said Joh Kutler of Quarterdeck Investment Partners, a company specialising in aerospace defence mergers and acquisitiions.
Raytheon has an advantage over Northrop because it could sell three non-defence units for as much as $6 billion to $7 billion, experts said.

At stake are Hughes businesses with annual revenues of about $6.2 billion. The assets include missile systems, radar and communications electronics, air traffic control systems and an electro-optical devices unit.
"This is the last big prize there is," said Thomas Meagher of brokerage Ferris Baker Watts. "Whoever gets (Hughes) becomes the third major player."
Boeing Co. and Lockheed Martin Corp. have become the biggest players in the ever-consolidating defence industry while smaller firms are scrambling to keep pace.
Meagher said further consolidation lies ahead.

"Regardless of who wins this, Raytheon and Northrop will be forced into some sort of alliance, maybe two or three years down the line, in order to become a viable competitor to Boeing and Lockheed Martin," he said.
"In the end, I think (Raytheon and Northrop) are going to be part of the same company," Meagher added.
